snip.t: T. brucei gambiense → West African Sleeping Sickness (WASS)
WASS: West African Sleeping Sickness = T.b. gambiense = Glossina palpalis

qs.q: Which specific physical finding is classically associated with posterior cervical lymphadenopathy in West African Sleeping Sickness?
qs.e: Winterbottom's sign refers to posterior cervical lymphadenopathy found in West African Sleeping Sickness. Romana's sign is instead associated with acute Chagas disease.

qs.q: Researchers are setting up traps in a known focus of West African sleeping sickness. Which tsetse fly species is the primary vector for Trypanosoma brucei gambiense?
qs.e: Glossina palpalis and G. tachinoides transmit West African sleeping sickness caused by T. b. gambiense. Glossina morsitans transmits the East African form.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: West African Sleeping Sickness is a chronic African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, transmitted by the tsetse fly. It progresses from a hemolymphatic stage to a meningo‑encephalitic stage with sleep disturbance and neuropsychiatric signs.

sections.p: A chronic parasitic disease endemic to West‑Central Africa, affecting rural populations with limited health resources. The parasite evades immunity by antigenic variation, leading to prolonged infection.
b: Incubation: weeks to months after bite
Two clinical stages: early (haemolymphatic) and late (CNS)

sections.p: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is a flagellated protozoan that lives extracellularly in blood, lymph, and later cerebrospinal fluid. It expresses a dense variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) coat that changes to avoid host antibodies.

Infection occurs when an infected Glossina palpalis (tsetse fly) takes a blood meal. Metacyclic trypomastigotes are injected, multiply in the skin, then enter blood and lymph. After months, they cross the blood‑brain barrier.

Early stage presents with intermittent fever, lymphadenopathy (especially posterior cervical ‘Winterbottom’s sign’), and mild headache. Late stage adds sleep disruption, personality change, gait disturbance, and eventually coma.
b: Stage I: parasites in blood/lymph, CSF <5 cells/µL, protein <45 mg/dL
Stage II: parasites in CSF, ≥5 cells/µL or protein ≥45 mg/dL

sections.p: Demonstration of parasites in body fluids is definitive. In low‑resource settings, microscopy of blood (wet mount, concentration) and lymph node aspirate are first steps; CSF analysis confirms CNS involvement.

t.a: Microscopy of blood or lymph node aspirate
t.b: Is the parasite present? Positive confirms infection; negative does not rule out early disease.
Has the disease entered the CNS? ≥5 cells/µL or protein ≥45 mg/dL indicates stage II; if unavailable, treat based on clinical suspicion.
Screening tool; positive suggests exposure but needs parasitological confirmation.

sections.p: Stage‑specific therapy: early stage with pentamidine (or suramin for T. b. rhodesiense); late stage with nifurtimox‑eflornithine combination (NECT) or fexinidazole where available. Supportive care includes antipyretics, nutrition, and monitoring for drug toxicity.
b: Pentamidine: chosen for good blood‑brain barrier exclusion, low toxicity
NECT: synergistic, reduces eflornithine dose, avoids severe hematologic toxicity of melarsoprol
Fexinidazole: oral option for both stages, limited by hepatic impairment

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: differentiate stage I vs II by CSF findings; know the vector and endemic geography; recall that T. b. gambiense causes a chronic disease, unlike the acute T. b. rhodesiense form.
b: CSF >5 cells/µL = indication for CNS‑penetrating drugs
Never use melarsoprol for T. b. gambiense unless NECT unavailable

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid neurological decline, seizures, coma, or severe sleep disturbance indicating late‑stage disease

faq.q: Why does the disease cause sleep disturbances?
faq.a: Parasites invade the hypothalamic sleep‑wake centers, disrupting circadian rhythms.

faq.q: Can the disease be cured without drugs?
faq.a: No; spontaneous clearance does not occur. Effective chemotherapy is required.
No; antigenic variation prevents a lasting vaccine response.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria that separate stage I from stage II African trypanosomiasis.
Explain why pentamidine is used for early‑stage disease but not for late‑stage disease.
List three public‑health measures to reduce transmission of West African sleeping sickness.
